title: Ten systems in your organization
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Ten systems that might be running in a large organization right now. Sort each one.

**Assembling** — gathering, structuring, summarizing, flagging for a human. **Deciding** — the system determines an outcome for a person, or a human approves something they cannot interrogate. **Prohibited** — the answer does not depend on how well it is done.

buckets.label: Assembling
buckets.hint: A named person still decides, on material they can interrogate

buckets.label: Deciding
buckets.hint: The system determines the outcome — or the human can't see inside it

tasks.text: A tool that summarizes 400 open-text engagement comments into themes for the leadership team
tasks.reasoning: Aggregate, no individual outcome, and the humans reading it can go back to the source. The clearest assembling card, and worth noting because most AI in HR should look like this.

tasks.text: Webcam-based attention scoring during virtual onboarding sessions, in a company with European operations
tasks.reasoning: The workplace emotion-recognition prohibition has been absolute since February 2025. Not a consent question and not a risk to manage. Note that products like this are marketed to People functions specifically, on the grounds that they finally measure engagement.

tasks.text: A screening tool that ranks applicants, where a recruiter reviews the top 20 and rejects the rest unopened
tasks.reasoning: The hardest card, and the most common real configuration. A human is technically in the loop, and they are approving a ranked list they cannot interrogate — everyone below the cut was rejected by the system. 101 M7's line: reviewing a ranked list is not the same as deciding.

tasks.text: An assistant that drafts interview questions from a job description for the hiring manager to edit
tasks.reasoning: Production of material a human then owns and can change entirely. Note the contrast with t3 — the same vendor may sell both, and the release note will describe them the same way.

tasks.text: Skills inference from work history that determines who appears in the internal talent marketplace
tasks.reasoning: Nobody experiences this as a decision system, which is exactly why it belongs here. An allocation of opportunity depends on the inference, the affected person usually cannot see their profile, and if it learned from who has historically been promoted it will reproduce that. The Talent Development track builds a whole lesson on this surface.

tasks.text: A scheduling system that routes interview slots, prioritizing candidates predicted most likely to accept
tasks.reasoning: Reads as logistics and shapes an outcome. Candidates deprioritized by the prediction get worse slots, longer waits, and a worse experience — which affects who stays in the process. The tell for this whole category: a system nobody would call a decision engine, doing allocation.

tasks.text: A model that flags performance review text likely to contain vague or coded language, for the manager to reconsider
tasks.reasoning: Aimed at the *writing* rather than at rating the person, and the manager remains the author. The distinction between AI reading what managers wrote and AI rating people is a real and teachable line.

tasks.text: An AI coaching tool available to all employees, with no escalation path and no stated policy on disclosures
tasks.reasoning: Arguable, and the argument is the point. It decides nothing directly — and by having no designed behaviour for a serious disclosure, the organization has made a decision by default that the vendor's configuration now enforces. The module's scenario in card form; the failure is that nobody chose.

tasks.text: Automated generation of the first draft of a redundancy selection matrix from performance and skills data
tasks.reasoning: 'First draft' does a great deal of work in that sentence. The matrix determines who is selected, and a human reviewing a generated matrix is reviewing a conclusion rather than constructing one. If this is to sit in assembling, the human has to be able to rebuild it from inputs — which is the comp track's rule arriving here.

tasks.text: A chatbot answering employee policy questions, deployed to staff in the EU, that does not identify itself as AI
tasks.reasoning: Not prohibited in substance — a policy chatbot is fine and useful. Prohibited *as configured*: since 2 August 2026 a system interacting directly with a person must disclose that it is AI at or before the start of the interaction, regardless of risk class. One configuration change moves this card to assembling, which is why it is worth finding before someone else does.
